name: RecurLocal
status: feasibility test COMPLETE on TWO models and they disagree, which is the finding. Dense Qwen3.8-27B: go/no-go reject, and the reason is arithmetic - the recurrent footprint a persisting cache would have to hold is 2.4x its capacity at batch 1 and 39.9x at 32 sequences, so the persist family tops out at 0.52% weighted against a 5.22% traffic ceiling. Sparse-MoE Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: the arithmetic inverts - a 3.56 GB decode step puts the footprint at 1.02x capacity, the batch-1 persist ceiling at 3.67% and measured batch-1 persist at +1.74% across three contexts, the largest real-model gain here. Weighted, the persist family reaches 1.94% against the 2.0% floor - six hundredths short, with both dials at maximum and a bound that already assumes perfect replacement. AND that result is not scorable at all: the MoE checkpoint is not reproducible against itself (two unhooked control runs diverge at token 1), so the exact-locality gate cannot certify it. RecurLocal is not the cause - the dense checkpoint is bit-identical across control, control and candidate on the same binary and policy. A reproducible MoE checkpoint is the first blocker on that surface
core: software-directed CUDA locality for mutable recurrent LLM state, embeddable in an inference runtime, with enumerated optimization surfaces measured against a real model rather than a microbenchmark
validated: CPU build, planner and decision tests (85 Python checks, 4 of them on the new quota policy validated by reverting it), 120 device-side controller checks on an RTX 5090, compute-sanitizer clean (memcheck/initcheck/synccheck/racecheck), install + find_package consumption, eval schema and pinned-integration validation, a COMPLETE section 44 workload matrix on Qwen3.8-27B/SparkInfer with token-exact output and the hook proven active, and a second model measured on the same pinned commit and box with three ceilings computed per arm (traffic, persist-family, within-layer) and the bandwidth-bound check that says how tight each one is
